newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mobutu names new army chief, gears up for war.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu names new army chief, gears up for war.

text.p: President Mobutu Sese Seko, in his first act since returning from a prolonged absence in Europe, has named a new army chief of staff -- bringing back a respected commander tested on the field of battle.

State television, announcing the appointment of General Mahele Bokoungo Lieko on Wednesday, said the move was intended to help Zaire's demoralised army meet the challenge of the Tutsi-led revolt in the east.

Mahele, sacked as army chief of staff by Mobutu in 1993, snuffed out a revolt by rebel leader Laurent Kabila in 1984 and helped fight Tutsi rebels who challenged Rwanda's late Hutu president Juvenal Habyarimana in 1990.
His nomination was "part of a restructuring of the Armed Forces of Zaire with the view to putting them on a war footing and improving their efficiency", the television said.
Mobutu, who spent four months in Europe for cancer surgery and rest, returned to a rapturous welcome on Tuesday and pledged to "restore Zaire's tarnished image".
The television said he would consult political leaders on Thursday.

The rebels, backed by neighbouring Rwanda, launched their revolt on October 18, accusing the Zairean authorities of denying citizenship to ethnic Tutsis who had lived there for generations. They hold towns and territory in the east.

Mobutu sacked Mahele, who is mistrusted by his peers but is popular among the troops and the population at large, after he criticised the army's role in Zaire and called for changes during a 1993 national conference on democratic change.
Since then, Mahele, who saw active service against Katangese secessionist forces in the mineral-rich southern province of Shaba in 1978, has kept a low profile.

Mobutu, who has dominated life in the sprawling and chaotic Central African nation since seizing power in 1965, shunted aside General Baramoto Kpama, who had only been in the post of chief of staff since last month.
Baramoto, commander of the feared civil guard, had been placed "at the disposition of the presidency", the television said. Command of the civil guard passed to little-known General Vungbo Ndepo.

Military sources said Mahele made two conditions for taking charge of the ill-disciplined army -- control of the entire military command, including the pampered presidential guard, and the power to sanction senior officers.
It was not clear if the conditions were granted.

Earlier, a close friend of Mobutu, who asked to remain anonymous, said military hardware, including 15 helicopters and several fighter jets, had been brought into Zaire in the past three weeks, accompanied by 154 foreign military personnel.
He declined to give details on their origin.
Baramoto replaced General Eluki Monga who accused the government of not giving the army the means to deal with the rebellion.
Eluki, the man who replaced Mahele in 1993, also publicly differed with the government in its call for an international force in Zaire.
